title: Chromosome-specific maturation of the epigenome in the Drosophila male germline

abstract: Spermatogenesis in the Drosophila male germline proceeds through a unique transcriptional program controlled both by germline-specific transcription factors and by testis-specific versions of core transcriptional machinery. This program includes the activation of genes on the heterochromatic Y chromosome, and reduced transcription from the X chromosome, but how expression from these sex chromosomes is regulated has not been defined. To resolve this, we profiled active chromatin features in the testes from wildtype and meiotic arrest mutants and integrate this with single-cell gene expression data from the Fly Cell Atlas. These data assign the timing of promoter activation for genes with germline-enriched expression throughout spermatogenesis, and general alterations of promoter regulation in germline cells. By profiling both active RNA polymerase II and histone modifications in isolated spermatocytes, we detail widespread patterns associated with regulation of the sex chromosomes. Our results demonstrate that the X chromosome is not enriched for silencing histone modifications, implying that sex chromosome inactivation does not occur in the Drosophila male germline. Instead, a lack of dosage compensation in spermatocytes accounts for the reduced expression from this chromosome. Finally, profiling uncovers dramatic ubiquitinylation of histone H2A and lysine-16 acetylation of histone H4 across the Y chromosome in spermatocytes that may contribute to the activation of this heterochromatic chromosome.

elife_assessment.summary: Using a variety of methods including mutant analyses, the authors study chromatin structure during spermatogenesis in Drosophila and transcriptional profiling in single cells/nuclei. This description of the dramatic changes in chromatin structure during spermatogenesis leads to some new observations, with convincing evidence, and it is useful for the field.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2023 eLife article has seen clear scholarly uptake: OpenAlex records 18 citations, placing it in the top 10% of cited works for its field and year. eLife’s assessment judged the study “Useful” with “Convincing” strength, and the downstream citation record suggests that the paper has been taken up quickly in the chromatin, dosage compensation, and Drosophila germline literature.

Full narrative

The article examines how the epigenome matures across chromosomes during spermatogenesis in the Drosophila male germline, focusing on the unusual regulation of the heterochromatic Y chromosome and the reduced transcription from the X chromosome. That biological problem has resonated with later work: citations appear across a concentrated set of venues in genetics and chromatin biology, including PLoS Genetics, bioRxiv, Science Advances, and related scholarly outlets. The citing literature is especially centered in genomics, chromatin dynamics, sex chromosome biology, and chromosomal variation, indicating that the paper has become part of an active research conversation rather than remaining a one-off observation.

The reuse profile also points to substantive scholarly reach. The article has 18 documented downstream reuses, mostly in journal articles, with additional reuse in preprints and book chapters. That pattern is consistent with rapid uptake: the paper was cited in the year of publication and then increasingly in the following years, with the citation record continuing into 2026. Several later studies on meiotic sex chromosome inactivation, meiotic drive, and other Drosophila chromatin questions draw on the same conceptual space, suggesting the work has helped frame how researchers think about sex-chromosome regulation during germline development.

The record also shows signs of careful, reusable scholarship. The article is open access, links to a Dryad dataset, and the repository and data citation trail indicate that the underlying materials were made available for reuse. RRID-linked resources are present in the article record, which supports reproducibility and makes the work easier to build on. In other words, the impact is not only in citation volume but also in the infrastructure for reuse and verification around the study.

Evidence of broader public discussion is limited in the collected sources, so the strongest story here is scholarly rather than popular impact. The paper’s influence is therefore best described as a well-received and methodologically grounded contribution to Drosophila chromatin biology: useful to the field, supported by convincing evidence, and already embedded in a growing network of follow-on research.
